raw.support_text: A comparative study of enzymic factors influencing metabolic inactivation of phenyloxirane (styrene oxide), a mutagenic metabolite of styrene, examined soluble glutathione S-transferase and microsomal epoxide hydratase in the 9000 x g supernatant (S9) of rat-liver homogenate, partly by the Ames test with S. typhimurium TA100. A gas-liquid chromatographic study indicated that the glutathione effect was attributable to disappearance of the mutagen from the microbial assay system; the rate of disappearance was 10-20 times as fast in the soluble supernatant fraction as in the microsomes when fortified with more than 4 mM glutathione. The results indicate cytosol glutathione S-transferase plays a much more important role than microsomal epoxide hydratase in detoxication of phenyloxirane.
raw.assay_method_and_endpoint: Gas-liquid chromatographic measurement of the rate of disappearance of phenyloxirane (styrene oxide) from the assay system, reflecting its metabolic inactivation (glutathione conjugation by soluble glutathione S-transferase)
raw.biological_system: Dialyzed soluble supernatant (cytosol) fraction vs microsomal fraction of the 9000 x g supernatant (S9) from male Wistar rat-liver homogenate (100-120 g rats)
raw.exposure_and_mechanistic_conditions: Phenyloxirane (styrene oxide) as the directly assayed test agent; fractions fortified with more than 4 mM glutathione; comparison of soluble supernatant vs microsomal preparations
raw.extra_details: Rate of phenyloxirane disappearance in the soluble supernatant was 10-20 times faster than in microsomes when fortified with ≥4 mM glutathione. The mutagenic-activity results (S. typhimurium TA100 revertants) are Ames-test data and are excluded here; only the independent GLC disappearance (detoxification) endpoint is extracted. Conclusion: cytosol glutathione S-transferase predominates over microsomal epoxide hydratase in detoxication.

raw.support_text: The metabolism of NO-HEX by rat and hamster S8 and S9 fractions was measured by the non-methylene chloride-extractable (NMCE) method.
